note: The two cases the issue names, split into two fixtures so a mismatch localizes. valid/symlinked-store makes tasks.jsonl a relative symlink to tasks.real.jsonl beside it: it is the only fixture that reaches Atomic.resolve's follow branch, and the only one where the sidecar names differ from the configured path — after a capture the tree holds tasks.jsonl (still a symlink, same target), tasks.real.jsonl (new bytes), and .tasks.real.jsonl.lock. Store#lock_path resolves through Journal.canonical and Atomic.write resolves through Atomic.resolve, two independent code paths that must reach the same answer; a port that names either sidecar from the configured path leaves an extra file the runner records as a delta. Unlike the 0600 bit, the symlink ships as bytes — git stores symlinks, cp -a preserves them, and root_sha256 already defines a symlink as contributing '-' in place of a digest, so no protocol change is needed for it. valid/restricted-mode-store is the copy_mode case: under umask 022 a fresh temp is born 0644, so without Atomic.copy_mode an atomic replace silently widens a private store to world-readable with no error, no warning, and not one byte of content changed — invisible to a byte comparator, visible only in files.after[].mode. Neither fixture touches porting/runners/; the protocol need is reported above rather than implemented. Suggested oracle_gaps addition for this slice: 'Atomic.resolve's dangling-symlink branch (readlink + expand_path when the target does not exist) is not reachable from a store fixture — a dangling link carries no store to read — and stays uncovered by the corpus.'

Add to "What was found while building this", as a fourth item:

**4. Sidecar names follow the symlink; the lock's mode does not follow the store's.** In `valid/symlinked-store` both the temp sibling and the lock resolve to the *target* name (`.tasks.real.jsonl.lock`), by two independent code paths — `Atomic.resolve` and `Journal.canonical`. In `valid/restricted-mode-store` the store keeps 0600 across the replace but `Store#with_lock` opens the lock with a literal `0o644`, so a deliberately private store acquires a world-readable sidecar. The sidecar is empty, so only its existence and mtime are exposed; recorded, not fixed.

note: The id-less stores go in malformed/, not compat/, and the argument is decidable rather than aesthetic: compat/ means bytes a different version of this binary legitimately wrote, and no version ever wrote an id-less task — ids are minted at capture and always have been. Check agrees in as many words: check_id emits 'record missing id' as an error, so the store is one the linter refuses, which is this class's definition. That makes ensure_id! the only mutation in the product expected to run against a file `check` fails. missing-id-single has exactly one id-less record and answers the three questions the slice must answer: `tasks list` does not repair (bytes identical, exit 0 — there is no lazy repair anywhere in the read path); `tasks capture` refuses before writing ('task file is already invalid … (nothing was written)'); `tasks id` repairs (exit 0, mints bbbb0001 into that record). missing-ids-many is the boundary the single-record fixture cannot show — with_history has no preflight, so ensure_id_impl mints one id, the post-write Check still fails on the other two, and the write is rolled back ('file failed validation after the edit'). The two wordings are how a port proves it kept the refusal and the rollback distinct: adding a preflight to ensure_id! looks like an optimization and would produce the wrong one. valid/id-pin-collision is the collision corpus, arranged against the pin the runner already sets (TASKS_PIN_IDS=bbbb0001): bbbb0001 and bbbb0002 sit in archive.jsonl and bbbb0003 in tasks.jsonl, so a capture must skip three and mint bbbb0004. Two *consecutive* archived collisions are deliberate — one collision proves a guard, two prove a loop — and the live-side one proves gen_id's taken set spans both files. Under SecureRandom that loop is unobservable, so a port that dropped the archive read, or the loop, would pass every other fixture in the corpus forever.

Add to "What was found while building this":

**Id repair is a record repair, not a store repair.** `Store#ensure_id!` is reachable from exactly one command (`tasks id`) — never from a read, never as a side effect of another write. It mints one id and then `with_history`'s post-write `Check` validates the *whole file*, so it converges only when that record was the file's last remaining error. A store with two id-less records has no command that can fix it; the only exit is a hand edit. Recorded, not fixed. Two further details a port must match: the repaired record gains an `updated` stamp, because `stamp_changed_tasks!` indexes by id and the just-minted id is in no original, so a repair is indistinguishable from a new task; and `tasks capture` on such a store reports `could not capture (no "Inbox" section found?)` as its first stderr line even when an Inbox is present — the true cause is the second line, from the `store_invalid?` branch, and the misleading first line is contract now.

note: An accept/reject pair, built after enumerating what lib/tasks/recur.rb actually accepts rather than from the issue's list alone. valid/recur-calendar-grammar carries twenty canonical forms, one per record — every axis beyond the six in full-field-matrix: weekly interval (2w:mon), the calendar one-hop prefix (+w:mon), all three together (+3w:tue,thu), the weekday and weekend sets, m:last, m:2tue, m:1,15, m:lastfri, 2m:5fri, m:1,last, m:31, y:11:3thu, 2y:02:5fri, +y:12-25, y:02-29, and multi-digit interval counts on all four units. malformed/recur-non-canonical is the half the issue did not ask for and the half that makes the slice falsifiable: twenty-seven rejections, one per record, in three groups. Group 1 is thirteen grammar violations. Group 2 is eleven values that PARSE but are not canonical — Recur.schedule accepts a stored string only when canonical_calendar reproduces it exactly, so 1w:mon, w:monday, w:wed,mon, w:mon,mon, m:01, m:15,1, m:2tues, y:7-04 and y:07-4 are all refused despite Recur.parse normalizing every one of them. That is the branch a port most easily gets wrong, because 'it parses' feels like enough, and lines 15 and 22 are the trap inside it: day-of-month is not zero-padded, the yearly month is. Group 3 is the two rows where Recur.cookie? and Check DISAGREE — ' w:mon' and 'w:mon ' are true to cookie? (it strips) and rejected by check_task's rc == rc.strip guard — plus an integer recur for the type guard that must report rather than raise. A port that validates recurrence by calling its own parser and nothing else accepts both padded rows and passes every other row in the file. Together with malformed/wrong-types the reject side is now the enumerated one rather than a single easy case. Month-end clamping is next-date math and correctly stays in campaign 5; nothing about it is asserted here.

Add to "What was found while building this":

**`Check` discards every reason `Recur` produced.** `Recur.parse_result` returns richly specific rejections — `day of month must be 1–31: "32"`, `unknown day of week: "xyz"`, the whole explanation of why `.+` cannot prefix a calendar schedule. `check_task` calls the boolean `Recur.cookie?` instead, so all twenty-seven rows of `malformed/recur-non-canonical` collapse into one message that varies only by the inspected value. On the `check` surface a port therefore owes `cookie?` fidelity only — accept/reject agreement and the one fixed message — and reproducing Ruby's per-reason wording there would be a divergence, not an improvement. Those messages *are* user-visible on the input surface (`tasks recur`, `Recur.explain`), which is a different slice: one grammar, validated twice, at two levels of diagnosis.
